notes: Garden Tracker spices guide: what part is the spice, climate by USDA zone, harvest, drying, storing and cooking. Own words, from extension, university, government and FAO sources.

groups.name: Sunny & dry (Mediterranean)
groups.tip: Full sun and soil that drains fast. Do not overwater.

groups.name: Moist soil
groups.tip: Rich soil that stays damp. Some like part shade.

groups.name: Seed spices
groups.tip: Sow right in the bed. Let plants go to seed.

groups.name: Hot & tangy
groups.tip: Warm sun. Dry the harvest well.

groups.name: Hot peppers
groups.tip: Mild to superhot. Warm soil to start. Wear gloves.

groups.name: Tropical spices
groups.tip: Need heat all year. In cold zones, grow in pots you bring inside or in a warm greenhouse.

spices.climate: Mild to warm, dry summers. Lives outside in zones 4–9.
spices.harvest: Cut stems just as flowers start to open.
spices.dry: Hang small bunches upside down in a dark, airy room. Leaves are dry when they crumble. NCHFP says a dehydrator at 95–115°F works too.
spices.store: Keep whole leaves in a closed jar in a dark, cool place. Crush just before you cook.

src.t: University of Missouri Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home
National Center for Home Food Preservation — Drying Herbs

spices.climate: Mild to warm, dry summers. Likes poor, well-drained soil.
spices.harvest: Cut the soft tips before it blooms.
spices.dry: Hang small bunches upside down in a dark, airy room. Leaves are dry when they crumble. NCHFP says a dehydrator at 95–115°F works too.
spices.store: Keep whole leaves in a closed jar in a dark, cool place. Crush just before you cook.

src.t: University of Missouri Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home
National Center for Home Food Preservation — Drying Herbs

spices.climate: Mild winters (zone 8 and up). Bring it in where winters are cold.
spices.harvest: Snip stem tips any time.
spices.dry: Hang small bunches upside down in a dark, airy room. Leaves are dry when they crumble. NCHFP says a dehydrator at 95–115°F works too.
spices.store: Keep whole leaves in a closed jar in a dark, cool place. Crush just before you cook.

src.t: University of Missouri Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home
National Center for Home Food Preservation — Drying Herbs

spices.climate: Cool to warm places with dry soil. Lives outside in zones 4–8.
spices.harvest: Pick leaves before it blooms. Do not cut much in the fall.
spices.dry: Hang small bunches upside down in a dark, airy room. Leaves are dry when they crumble. NCHFP says a dehydrator at 95–115°F works too.
spices.store: Keep whole leaves in a closed jar in a dark, cool place. Crush just before you cook.

src.t: University of Illinois Extension — Sage
University of Missouri Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home
National Center for Home Food Preservation — Drying Herbs

spices.climate: Lives outside only where winters are mild (zones 9–10). Grow it each year elsewhere.
spices.harvest: Cut stems when flower buds form.
spices.dry: Hang small bunches upside down in a dark, airy room. Leaves are dry when they crumble. NCHFP says a dehydrator at 95–115°F works too.
spices.store: Keep whole leaves in a closed jar in a dark, cool place. Crush just before you cook.
spices.uses: Eggs, soups, sauces. Milder than oregano.

src.t: University of Illinois Extension — Sweet Marjoram
University of Missouri Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home
National Center for Home Food Preservation — Drying Herbs

spices.climate: Any place with a warm summer. Grow it each year.
spices.harvest: Cut stems before it blooms.
spices.dry: Hang small bunches upside down in a dark, airy room. Leaves are dry when they crumble. NCHFP says a dehydrator at 95–115°F works too.
spices.store: Keep whole leaves in a closed jar in a dark, cool place. Crush just before you cook.

src.t: University of Illinois Extension — Summer Savory
University of Missouri Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home

spices.climate: Cool to mild places (zones 4–8). Does poorly in hot, wet summers.
spices.harvest: Pick leaves from early summer on.
spices.dry: Hang to dry, or freeze leaves. Drying loses some taste.
spices.store: Keep whole leaves in a closed jar in a dark, cool place. Crush just before you cook.

src.t: University of Illinois Extension — French Tarragon
University of Missouri Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home

spices.climate: Mild winters (zone 8 and up). Grow in a pot and bring it in elsewhere.
spices.harvest: Pick older leaves any time.
spices.dry: Lay leaves flat in a dry, shady spot.
spices.store: Store whole in a jar. Take leaves out of food before eating.

src.t: University of Missouri Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home
National Center for Home Food Preservation — Drying Herbs

spices.climate: Cold winters are OK (zones 5–8) but summers must be dry. Use a pot in wet places.
spices.harvest: Pick open flowers on a dry morning. Pull out the 3 red threads.
spices.dry: Dry threads on paper in a warm room for a few days.
spices.store: Keep in a tiny closed jar in the dark.
spices.uses: Rice, paella, bread, soups. A pinch goes far.

src.t: University of Vermont — Saffron planting for home gardeners
University of Kentucky CCD — Saffron

spices.companions: Plant in a sunny, dry spot. Mark where corms are so you do not dig them up.

spices.climate: Cool to warm places with moist soil (zones 3–8).
spices.harvest: Cut stems just before flowers open.
spices.dry: Hang small bunches upside down in a dark, airy room. Leaves are dry when they crumble. NCHFP says a dehydrator at 95–115°F works too.
spices.store: Keep whole leaves in a closed jar in a dark, cool place. Crush just before you cook.

src.t: University of Missouri Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home
National Center for Home Food Preservation — Drying Herbs

spices.companions: Mint spreads fast. Grow it in a pot or a buried pot.

spices.climate: Cool weather. Lives two years.
spices.harvest: Cut outer stems.
spices.dry: Freezing keeps more taste than drying.
spices.store: Keep whole leaves in a closed jar in a dark, cool place. Crush just before you cook.

src.t: University of Missouri Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home
National Center for Home Food Preservation — Drying Herbs

spices.climate: Cold-hardy almost everywhere (zones 3–9).
spices.harvest: Snip leaves near the ground.
spices.dry: Chives freeze better than they dry.
spices.store: Freeze chopped chives in a bag.

src.t: University of Missouri Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home
National Center for Home Food Preservation — Drying Herbs

spices.climate: Cool places with moist soil.
spices.harvest: Pick leaves any time. Cut seed heads when brown.
spices.dry: Cut seed heads when most seeds turn brown. Hang them head down in a paper bag. Rub out the seeds when dry.
spices.store: Keep whole leaves in a closed jar in a dark, cool place. Crush just before you cook.

src.t: University of Missouri Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home

spices.climate: Cool places (zones 4–9). Rest in hot summers.
spices.harvest: Pick young leaves.
spices.dry: Best fresh. Freeze chopped leaves.
spices.store: Fresh in the fridge for a few days.

src.t: University of Illinois Extension — French Sorrel
University of Minnesota Extension — Growing sorrel

spices.warn: Sorrel has oxalic acid. Eat it in small amounts.

spices.climate: Cold winters are good (zones 4–9).
spices.harvest: Dig roots in late fall after frost.
spices.dry: Grate fresh root into white vinegar. It keeps a few weeks in the fridge. Roots can also be dried and ground.
spices.store: Store whole roots cold (32–40°F) in damp sand or the fridge.

src.t: Utah State University Extension — Horseradish in the Garden
University of Minnesota Extension — Growing horseradish

spices.companions: Plant it in a corner or a buried tub. Any root piece left behind grows back.
spices.warn: Grate it outdoors or by an open window. The fumes sting eyes.

spices.climate: Cool and shady (zones 7–10). Hates heat over about 80°F. Use a cool greenhouse or pot elsewhere.
spices.harvest: Dig the whole plant in spring or fall after about 2 years.
spices.dry: Grate fresh right before eating.
spices.store: Wrap the stem in a damp towel in the fridge.

src.t: Utah State University Extension — Wasabi in the Garden
Washington State University Extension — Wasabi
NC State Extension Plant Toolbox — Wasabi

spices.companions: Grow under trees or a shade cloth. Watch for slugs.

spices.climate: Cool weather. Bolts in heat. In hot places, grow it in the cool season.
spices.harvest: Pick leaves young. Let some plants go to seed for coriander.
spices.dry: Cut seed heads when most seeds turn brown. Hang them head down in a paper bag. Rub out the seeds when dry.
spices.store: Keep seeds in a closed jar, cool and dark. Grind just before you cook.
spices.uses: Leaves: salsa, curry. Seeds: pickles, curry, bread.

src.t: University of Missouri Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home
National Center for Home Food Preservation — Drying Herbs

spices.climate: Cool to warm summers.
spices.harvest: Cut leaves any time. Cut seed heads when seeds turn brown.
spices.dry: Cut seed heads when most seeds turn brown. Hang them head down in a paper bag. Rub out the seeds when dry.
spices.store: Keep seeds in a closed jar, cool and dark. Grind just before you cook.

src.t: University of Missouri Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home
National Center for Home Food Preservation — Drying Herbs

spices.companions: Keep dill away from fennel. They can cross.

spices.climate: Warm summers. Lives a few years where winters are mild.
spices.harvest: Cut seed heads when the seeds turn tan.
spices.dry: Cut seed heads when most seeds turn brown. Hang them head down in a paper bag. Rub out the seeds when dry.
spices.store: Keep seeds in a closed jar, cool and dark. Grind just before you cook.

src.t: University of Missouri Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home

spices.companions: Fennel slows some plants near it. Give it its own spot.

spices.climate: Cool places (zones 4–9). Lives two years.
spices.harvest: Cut seed heads the second summer when seeds turn brown.
spices.dry: Cut seed heads when most seeds turn brown. Hang them head down in a paper bag. Rub out the seeds when dry.
spices.store: Keep seeds in a closed jar, cool and dark. Grind just before you cook.

src.t: University of Missouri Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home
NC State Extension Plant Toolbox — Caraway

spices.climate: Needs a long warm season, about 4 months.
spices.harvest: Cut seed heads when seeds turn gray-brown.
spices.dry: Cut seed heads when most seeds turn brown. Hang them head down in a paper bag. Rub out the seeds when dry.
spices.store: Keep seeds in a closed jar, cool and dark. Grind just before you cook.

src.t: University of Missouri Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home
UF/IFAS Osceola County — Herb Planting Calendar

spices.climate: Needs a long, warm, dry season, about 5 months.
spices.harvest: Cut plants when seeds turn brown.
spices.dry: Cut seed heads when most seeds turn brown. Hang them head down in a paper bag. Rub out the seeds when dry.
spices.store: Keep seeds in a closed jar, cool and dark. Grind just before you cook.

src.t: UF/IFAS Osceola County — Herb Planting Calendar

spices.climate: Cool weather. Takes light frost.
spices.harvest: Pick leaves young. Pull plants when the pods dry.
spices.dry: Hang plants to dry. Shell out the seeds.
spices.store: Keep seeds in a closed jar, cool and dark. Grind just before you cook.
spices.uses: Curry, bread, pickles. Soak seeds to tame the bitter taste.

src.t: UC Master Gardeners (Santa Clara) — Fenugreek
Penn State PlantVillage — Fenugreek
UVM Extension — Spice up your garden with Asian flavors

spices.climate: Cool weather. Fast grower.
spices.harvest: Cut plants when most pods turn tan, before they split.
spices.dry: Cut seed heads when most seeds turn brown. Hang them head down in a paper bag. Rub out the seeds when dry.
spices.store: Keep seeds in a closed jar, cool and dark. Grind just before you cook.

src.t: University of Missouri Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home

spices.climate: Hot summers. Needs about 4 warm months.
spices.harvest: Cut stalks when the lower pods turn yellow.
spices.dry: Stand stalks upside down in a bag to catch seeds.
spices.store: Keep seeds airtight and cool. They can go stale.

src.t: University of Missouri Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home

spices.climate: Warm summers. Lives for years in frost-free places.
spices.harvest: Pick when fully red.
spices.dry: String them into a hanging chain, or dry in a dehydrator until they snap.
spices.store: Keep dry peppers or flakes in a closed jar. Use within about 6 months for best taste.

src.t: Iowa State Extension — How can I dry hot peppers?
National Center for Home Food Preservation — Drying Herbs

spices.warn: Wear gloves when cutting or grinding hot peppers.

spices.climate: Warm summers.
spices.harvest: Pick fully red, thin-walled peppers.
spices.dry: Slice and dry until crisp, then grind into paprika.
spices.store: Keep paprika in a closed jar, cool and dark.

src.t: Iowa State Extension — How can I dry hot peppers?
National Center for Home Food Preservation — Drying Herbs

spices.climate: Needs a cold spell to make bulbs. In warm places choose softneck types.
spices.harvest: Dig when lower leaves turn brown.
spices.dry: Cure bulbs in a dry, shady, airy place for 2 to 3 weeks.
spices.store: Keep cured bulbs cool and dry with air around them.

src.t: University of Missouri Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home

spices.climate: Cold winters are fine (zones 3–8).
spices.harvest: Pick the fuzzy red clusters in late summer.
spices.dry: Dry clusters, then rub off the berries and grind.
spices.store: Keep the powder in a closed jar.
spices.uses: Sprinkle on salads, rice and meat for a lemon taste. Soak berries in cold water for a drink.

src.t: Michigan State University Extension — Making sumac tea

spices.warn: Only pick upright, fuzzy RED clusters. Poison sumac has white berries.

spices.climate: Cold winters are OK (zones 5–9).
spices.harvest: Pick the red fruits when ripe.
spices.dry: Dry fruits until the husks split. Throw out the black seeds.
spices.store: Keep seeds in a closed jar, cool and dark. Grind just before you cook.
spices.uses: Stir-fry, noodles, chili oil. Makes your mouth tingle.

src.t: NC State Extension Plant Toolbox — Sichuan pepper

spices.warn: Thorny stems. Wear gloves.

spices.climate: Warm and moist (zones 8–10). A pot works in colder places.
spices.harvest: Dig when leaves turn yellow, about 8 to 10 months.
spices.dry: Slice thin and dry, or freeze pieces.
spices.store: Fridge for weeks, or freeze.

src.t: UF/IFAS EP638 — Ginger, Galangal, and Turmeric Production in Florida
FAO — Herbs, spices and essential oils: post-harvest operations

spices.climate: Warm and moist (zones 8–10). A pot works in colder places.
spices.harvest: Dig when leaves die back.
spices.dry: Boil, slice and dry, then grind into powder.
spices.store: Fridge for weeks, or freeze.

src.t: UF/IFAS EP638 — Ginger, Galangal, and Turmeric Production in Florida
FAO — Herbs, spices and essential oils: post-harvest operations

spices.climate: Loves heat. Dies at the first frost.
spices.harvest: Pinch stem tips often.
spices.dry: Freezing or pesto keeps more taste than drying.
spices.store: Keep whole leaves in a closed jar in a dark, cool place. Crush just before you cook.

src.t: University of Missouri Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home
National Center for Home Food Preservation — Drying Herbs

spices.climate: Tropical (zones 9–11). Use a pot and bring it in elsewhere.
spices.harvest: Cut stalks at least ½ in thick at ground level.
spices.dry: Dry leaves for tea. Freeze stalks.
spices.store: Frozen stalks keep about 6 months.

src.t: Utah State University Extension — Lemongrass in the Garden
University of Illinois Extension — Lemon Grass

spices.climate: Hot and wet (zones 9–12). A big pot works elsewhere.
spices.harvest: Dig young pieces at about 4 months.
spices.dry: Slice and freeze. Drying is possible.
spices.store: Freeze slices in a bag.

src.t: UF/IFAS EP638 — Ginger, Galangal, and Turmeric Production in Florida
UF/IFAS Osceola County — Gingers for your garden

spices.climate: Warm places (zones 10–13). Pot it and bring it in when it freezes.
spices.harvest: Pick fresh leaves any time.
spices.dry: Fresh leaves taste best. Freeze extras.
spices.store: Freeze leaves in a bag.
spices.uses: Fry in oil for curry, dal and rice.

src.t: UF/IFAS Charlotte County — Curry leaf

spices.warn: Do not eat the seeds.

spices.climate: Hot, humid shade, about 65–95°F. Needs a warm greenhouse outside the tropics.
spices.harvest: Pick green pods just before they ripen.
spices.dry: FAO: dry pods slowly in warm air until they rattle.
spices.store: Keep pods whole in a jar.

src.t: NC State Extension Plant Toolbox — Cardamom
FAO — Herbs, spices and essential oils: post-harvest operations

spices.climate: Hot, wet tropics (zones 11–13). A heated greenhouse elsewhere.
spices.harvest: Snip the spikes when a few berries turn red.
spices.dry: Sun-dry green berries until black and wrinkled.
spices.store: Keep seeds in a closed jar, cool and dark. Grind just before you cook.

src.t: University of Hawaii CTAHR — Black pepper fact sheet
FAO — Herbs, spices and essential oils: post-harvest operations

spices.climate: Hot, humid tropics about 75–85°F (zones 11–13). A warm greenhouse elsewhere.
spices.harvest: Pick pods when the tips start to yellow, 7 to 9 months after the flowers.
spices.dry: Pods must be cured for weeks: warmed, sweated and slowly dried until brown.
spices.store: Keep cured beans wrapped airtight.

src.t: UF/IFAS Gardening Solutions — Vanilla
FAO — Herbs, spices and essential oils: post-harvest operations

spices.climate: Warm, wet tropics (zones 10–12). A warm greenhouse elsewhere.
spices.harvest: Cut young stems, then peel the inner bark.
spices.dry: Bark curls into quills as it dries in the shade.
spices.store: Keep sticks in a closed jar.

src.t: NC State Extension Plant Toolbox — Cinnamon
FAO — Herbs, spices and essential oils: post-harvest operations

spices.climate: Warm tropics (zones 10–12). A warm greenhouse elsewhere.
spices.harvest: Pick full-size green berries.
spices.dry: Dry berries in the sun until brown and hard.
spices.store: Keep seeds in a closed jar, cool and dark. Grind just before you cook.

src.t: UF/IFAS Environmental Horticulture — Allspice (Pimenta dioica)
FAO — Herbs, spices and essential oils: post-harvest operations

spices.climate: Tropics (zones 10–11). A pot you bring in elsewhere.
spices.harvest: Pick pods when they turn brown and dry.
spices.dry: Dry the pods, then shake out the red seeds.
spices.store: Keep seeds in a closed jar, cool and dark. Grind just before you cook.
spices.uses: Colors rice, cheese and stews yellow-orange.

src.t: University of Guam Extension — Achiote
UF/IFAS Miami-Dade — Lipstick tree (Bixa orellana)

spices.climate: Warm summers. Grow it each year. Lives longer only where it never freezes (zones 10–11).
spices.harvest: Pick young leaves all summer.
spices.dry: Best fresh. Leaves can be dried for tea.
spices.store: Keep whole leaves in a closed jar in a dark, cool place. Crush just before you cook.

src.t: UVM Extension — Spice up your garden with Asian flavors
NC State Extension Plant Toolbox — Perilla (shiso)

spices.companions: Grow it in a pot. Pinch off flowers before they make seeds.
spices.warn: Shiso spreads and is listed as invasive in some US states, so check your local rules. Grow it in pots and pinch flowers before they seed. It is toxic to cattle and horses, so keep it away from farm animals.

spices.climate: Warm places (zones 10–11). A pot or yearly plant elsewhere.
spices.harvest: Pick leaves in fall when they are sweetest. Pinch flower buds.
spices.dry: Hang bunches to dry. Dry leaves are sweeter.
spices.store: Crush and store airtight.

src.t: UF/IFAS Gardening Solutions — Stevia
NC State Extension Plant Toolbox — Stevia

spices.climate: Warm summers. To keep a plant over winter, cut it back, pot it, and keep it cool (50–60°F) and almost dry inside.
spices.harvest: Pick small and green. To save seed, keep kinds 400 ft apart or bag a flower.
spices.dry: String them up, or use a dehydrator until they snap.
spices.store: Keep dry pods or flakes in a closed jar.

spices.dry: String them up, or use a dehydrator until they snap.
spices.store: Keep dry pods or flakes in a closed jar.

items: Pick in the morning after the dew dries.
Cut leafy herbs just as flower buds open.
Cut seed heads when most seeds turn brown.
Rinse only if dirty, then shake dry.
Hang small bunches in a dark, airy room.
Put seed heads upside down in paper bags.
Check that leaves crumble and seeds are hard.
Store in closed jars, away from heat and light.
Write the name and date on each jar.
Use dried spices within about a year.
